title: Effects of reducing appearance related behaviours on body dysmorphic symptoms in university students at risk of body dysmorphic disorder
official: Effects of reducing appearance related behaviours on body dysmorphic symptoms in university students at risk of body dysmorphic disorder: a randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a mental health condition in which people worry a great deal about perceived flaws in their appearance and often feel very anxious and ashamed. BDD usually starts when people are teenagers and young adults. Without treatment, it can seriously affect people's lives. People with BDD are more likely to struggle in education and are at higher risk of suicide compared to people without the condition. 
There are effective treatments for BDD, but very few people receive treatment when they need it. We urgently need to develop interventions to help people earlier, before they develop BDD. 
This study aims to test an early intervention strategy for university students who are worried about their appearance, and whose worries are starting to get in the way of their lives. The intervention is based on a treatment already known to work for BDD (namely Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for BDD); it involves a brief 5-minute psycho-educational video, a brief therapeutic technique to practice daily, and daily text reminders. We aim to find out whether the intervention is better at reducing symptoms of BDD compared to an similar control condition.

Who can participate?
People can take part if they: 
1. Aged 18 years or older (there is no upper age limit)
2. Are registered UCL students
3. Have elevated but subclinical symptoms of BDD (this means they are unlikely to have BDD but their symptoms are still impairing)
4. Have not started or changed medication for a mental health condition in the past 6 weeks

What does the study involve?
Participants will first complete some questionnaires which assess whether they are eligible to be take part in the study. Then, they will be randomly assigned to either the intervention or the control condition. The group assigned to the intervention will watch a brief (about 5 minutes) video about the role of appearance related behaviours in maintaining appearance related concerns, are given a brief therapeutic technique to practice daily for 4 weeks and are sent text reminders every day for 4 weeks. Participants assigned to the control condition will also watch a brief video about the role of sleep in appearance anxiety, are given a brief therapeutic technique to practice daily for four weeks and are then sent text reminders every day for 4 weeks, as with the intervention condition. Each week both groups will be asked to complete a brief set of questionnaires. This will allow researchers to assess changes in BDD symptoms, and other mental health symptoms, and whether the participants in the intervention condition report greater improvement in BDD symptoms after 2 weeks compared to the control condition.
We are also interested to see whether the intervention and control are feasible (based on the number of participants recruited and retained in the study), acceptable to participants and are not associated with harmful effects. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may benefit from taking part if the intervention helps them feel less BDD symptoms, but, this cannot be guaranteed. Any participant who completes all data collection will be entered into a prize draw for £200. 
Some participants may find part of the intervention or control condition uncomfortable because it involves changing behaviours, which could lead to temporary feelings of anxiety or discomfort. 

Where is the study run from?
University College London (UCL) (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 to December 2027

Who is funding the study?
UCL Grand Challenge for Mental Health and Wellbeing (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Prof. Georgina Krebs, g.krebs@ucl.ac.uk

interventions.name: Participants will comprise of university students who report elevated but subthreshold body dysmorphic disorder symptoms as assessed by the Body Image Questionnaire (BIQ). Participants will be recruited from a community sample in University College London using physical adverts, digital advertising

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 18 years and over (there is no upper age limit)
2. Score between 20 and 39 on the Body Image Questionnaire (BIQ)
3. Be a UCL-registered student
Exclusion criteria:
1. BIQ score of less than 20 or 40 and above
2. Not be taking any new or have changed medications for a mental health condition within the previous 6 weeks
